title: From well to pump: how fuel prices are formed
gist: The ECB decomposes euro area pump prices into crude, refining margins, distribution, excise and VAT to show that the 2026 Middle East oil shock passed through to retail diesel fast and fully in level terms (+€0.55/litre, to €2.18 in early April), but only ~34% in relative terms because taxes and fixed costs dampen elasticity to roughly 0.3. The distinguishing feature of this shock is refining margins: the Strait of Hormuz closure knocked out enough refining capacity to push margin contributions from €0.10 to €0.35 per litre of diesel, amplifying the crude move and driving euro area energy HICP from -3.1% in February to 10.8% in May.

insights.claim: The ECB finds that crude oil price increases pass through to euro area pre-tax pump prices fast (within one to two months) and fully, with a €0.10 per litre rise in crude translating into a €0.10 per litre rise in pre-tax pump prices rather than being absorbed by retailer margins.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Model retail fuel inflation as a near-mechanical lagged function of Brent in euro terms; do not assume margin compression at the forecourt buffers consumers.
insights.quote: Rather than being absorbed by lower profit margins, an increase of €0.10 per litre in crude oil prices usually translates into an increase of €0.10 per litre in pre-tax pump prices.
insights.locator: Oil price rises are transmitted fast and fully

insights.claim: Brent crude rose rapidly in March 2026 after the outbreak of the Middle East conflict and peaked at 138 US dollars per barrel in early April, almost double the level seen in late February.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Anchors the size of the 2026 supply shock: a near-doubling of crude in roughly six weeks is the input to any energy-inflation or consumer-squeeze scenario.
insights.quote: Prices for Brent crude rose rapidly in March after the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, peaking at 138 US dollars per barrel in early April
insights.locator: To better understand how the recent oil price shock

insights.claim: Refined diesel prices outran crude during the 2026 shock, peaking at 197 US dollars per barrel in April versus 138 dollars for Brent, signalling that the refining stage rather than the wellhead was the marginal price setter.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Crack spreads, not flat price, captured the incremental value in this shock — exposure to refiners beats exposure to producers in a capacity-constrained supply crunch.
insights.quote: prices of diesel after the refining process rose even faster than prices of crude oil, peaking at 197 US dollars per barrel in April
insights.locator: To produce diesel, crude oil is processed in a refinery

insights.claim: Euro area retail diesel averaged €2.18 per litre in the first week of April 2026 versus €1.63 per litre in late February, a jump of roughly one third in about six weeks.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A €0.55 per litre hit to household transport budgets is a direct drag on discretionary consumption and a support for real-income-sensitive shorts in euro area consumer names.
insights.quote: By the first week of April, retail diesel prices averaged €2.18 per litre across the euro area compared with €1.63 per litre in late February – a sizeable jump of a third.
insights.locator: This resulted in ever higher prices at the pump

insights.claim: Diesel pump prices rose €0.55 per litre while the crude component rose only €0.35 per litre during the February-to-April 2026 shock, meaning the level pass-through was more than complete because of the extra contribution from refining.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Forecasting pump prices off crude alone would have understated the move by roughly 40 percent; refining spreads must be modelled separately.
insights.quote: this also helps us comprehend why diesel prices rose by €0.55 against only €0.35 for crude prices
insights.locator: While the pass-through from oil prices to pump prices is complete

insights.claim: Crude and refined diesel prices rose over 90% between end-February and the first week of April 2026, while euro area diesel prices at the pump rose only about 34%, because a large share of the retail price is fixed and does not move with oil market prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Headline oil moves must be haircut by roughly two-thirds before mapping into consumer fuel inflation in Europe.
insights.quote: The prices of crude oil and refined diesel rose by over 90% between the end of February and the first week of April (peak since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict), whereas diesel prices at the pump increased by around “only” 34%
insights.locator: In relative terms, retail prices increase less

insights.claim: The ECB uses a rule-of-thumb elasticity of around 0.3 for euro area retail fuel prices to oil prices — a 1% oil move produces a 0.3% retail move — consistent with its short-term energy inflation forecasting model (Working Paper No 3062).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A tradeable heuristic for sizing euro area energy HICP surprises off Brent moves, though the ECB warns the elasticity shifts with the level of each component.
insights.quote: an elasticity of around 0.3 (a 1% increase in oil prices leading to a 0.3% increase in retail prices) is in line with a short-term forecasting model for energy (and transport fuels) inflation in the euro area
insights.locator: While the elasticity of retail prices to oil prices changes

insights.claim: The ECB decomposes the euro area pump price into five components with distinct elasticities: crude oil, refining costs and margins, distribution costs and margins, excise duties and VAT.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Gives a component-level template for attributing any future fuel price move to shock, margin or policy — each with a different persistence and tradability.
insights.quote: Price elasticities – how much retail prices change in percentage terms when input prices change – vary along the five components that make up the price at the petrol station
insights.locator: Price elasticities – how much retail prices change

insights.claim: The crude oil component of euro area diesel has averaged around €0.47 per litre since 2021 within a €0.28 to €0.80 range, and reached €0.73 in the first week of April 2026, a 92% increase versus end-February.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The April peak sat near the top of the five-year historical band, implying limited further upside from the crude leg alone without a new escalation.
insights.quote: Since 2021 the crude oil component has averaged around €0.47 per litre of diesel, ranging from €0.28 to €0.80. At its most recent peak in the first week of April, it reached €0.73
insights.locator: Crude oil is highly sensitive to both supply shocks

insights.claim: Excise duties on euro area fuel are levied as a fixed amount per litre that rarely changes, averaging €0.52 for diesel and €0.66 for petrol since 2021, which is the main structural reason percentage pass-through to the pump is muted.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The fixed tax wedge acts as a built-in stabiliser for relative fuel inflation — countries with lower excise (outside Europe) see larger percentage pump swings from the same crude shock.
insights.quote: Excise duties are taxes levied at a fixed amount per litre that rarely changes, averaging €0.52 (diesel) and €0.66 (petrol) in the euro area since 2021.
insights.locator: Excise duties are taxes levied at a fixed amount

insights.claim: VAT on euro area fuel runs at roughly 19-22% in most countries and accounts for about one-sixth of the retail price, rising and falling with the pre-tax price but adding no independent volatility.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: VAT mechanically amplifies the euro-per-litre move by ~20% but is not itself a source of surprise, so it can be netted out when forecasting shocks.
insights.quote: Thus, they rise and fall with the pre-tax price but add no independent volatility. VAT accounts for roughly one-sixth of the retail price.
insights.locator: Value added taxes (VAT) are levied as a fixed percentage

insights.claim: Distribution costs and margins absorbed part of the 2026 shock, falling 14% versus end-February, so the retail and logistics stage was the only link in the chain that compressed rather than expanded.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Fuel retailers and distributors take margin pain in a crude spike; refiners take the gain — a clean pairs-trade logic within the downstream chain.
insights.quote: Distribution margins absorbed part of the increase in diesel refining, falling by 14% compared with the end of February.
insights.locator: Distribution costs and margins cover all activities

insights.claim: Refining costs and margins contributed €0.13 to the euro area retail diesel price in the last week of February 2026, in line with the average since 2021, and then rose 168% during the shock, making them the single most amplified component.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The €0.13 per litre historical baseline is the mean-reversion anchor for judging how much of any pump price is transient margin versus persistent crude.
insights.quote: In the last week of February, they contributed €0.13 to the retail price of diesel, in line with the historical average from 2021.
insights.locator: Refining costs and margins are calculated as the difference

insights.claim: Euro area diesel refining costs and margins jumped from a monthly average of €0.10 per litre in February 2026 to €0.26 in March, then surged to near-record highs contributing €0.35 per litre of diesel and €0.23 per litre of petrol over the first three weeks of July.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Near-record crack spreads are the clearest earnings signal in the complex; monitor whether they hold or mean-revert toward the €0.10-0.13 norm.
insights.quote: jumping from a monthly average of €0.10 per litre of diesel in February to €0.26 in March
insights.locator: This sharp supply crunch resulted in rapidly widening

insights.claim: The ECB lists the structural drivers of refining margin variability as differing refining processes and crude slates, and shifts in supply and demand for individual refined products caused by maintenance closures, conflict damage or political embargoes on specific countries' products.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A checklist for anticipating crack-spread blowouts: track outage schedules, conflict damage to refineries and sanctions on product flows, not just crude balances.
insights.locator: These margins may vary for a number of reasons

insights.claim: The renewed escalation of the Middle East conflict since early July 2026 pushed euro area retail diesel back up to around €1.98 per litre in the third week of July, with refining margins again the key driver rather than crude alone.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The second leg confirms the pattern is repeatable — refining capacity, not barrels in the ground, is the binding constraint in this cycle.
insights.quote: The renewed escalation of the conflict since early July has pushed pump prices back up, to around €1.98 per litre of diesel in the third week of July – with refining margins again playing an important role
insights.locator: The renewed escalation of the conflict since early July

themes.theme: Hormuz closure and the global refining capacity crunch

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in 2026 affected a significant share of global refining capacity and cut global refined-product exports by around 4.5 million barrels per day in the second quarter, according to the IEA's May 2026 Oil Market Report.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The shock transmitted through product exports, not just crude flows — the trade to express is product cracks and shipping of refined barrels, not simply long Brent.
insights.quote: the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has affected a significant share of global refining capacity. Essentially, this led to a decline in global refined-product exports of around 4.5 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026.
insights.locator: In the case of the recent energy shock, the closure

insights.claim: The IEA's July 2026 Oil Market Report shows global refinery runs down 6 million barrels per day year on year, with Middle East export refineries yet to restart, Russian throughputs curtailed by attacks and Asian refineries still running at reduced rates.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Three independent sources of lost runs means restoration is slow and staggered — the margin squeeze has structural legs beyond a single ceasefire headline.
insights.quote: global refinery runs are down 6 mb/d year on year, with Middle East export refineries yet to restart, Russian throughputs curtailed by attacks and Asia still running at reduced rates
insights.locator: According to International Energy Agency’s Oil Market Report

themes.theme: Forward path and asymmetric pass-through on the way down

insights.claim: Based on refined diesel futures as of 20 July 2026, the ECB expects the refining margin contribution to euro area diesel prices to peak in August 2026 and then decline to €0.16 per litre by end-2027, close to end-February 2026 levels.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The forward curve already prices normalisation over roughly 18 months — refiner earnings expectations beyond 2026 rest on that curve being too pessimistic.
insights.quote: based on refined diesel futures on 20 July, the contribution from margins is expected to peak in August before declining to €0.16 by the end of 2027, close to levels observed at the end of February 2026
insights.locator: Looking ahead, based on refined diesel futures

insights.claim: Crude oil prices fell significantly during the short-lived reopening of the Strait of Hormuz between 18 June and 11 July 2026, and euro area retail diesel prices followed suit, showing the transmission works in both directions.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Chokepoint status is the single highest-frequency variable for European fuel inflation this cycle — reopening headlines move the HICP within weeks.
insights.quote: Crude oil prices fell significantly during the recent short-lived reopening of the Strait of Hormuz (18 June to 11 July), and retail diesel prices followed suit
insights.locator: What happens on the “way down”?

insights.claim: Earlier euro area studies of the 'rockets and feathers' hypothesis found no asymmetry or were inconclusive, but the ECB notes that more recent work suggests pass-through could be slower when oil prices fall than when they rise.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: If downward stickiness is real, disinflation from falling crude arrives later than models assume — a reason to fade fast dovish repricing on oil declines.
insights.quote: Earlier studies for the euro area failed to find any asymmetries or the overall picture was inconclusive.
insights.locator: Over the last few decades the “rockets and feathers”

insights.claim: The ECB offers three candidate mechanisms for slower downward pass-through at the pump: lags in inventory replacement, uncertainty about whether crude price falls are persistent, and weaker competitive pressure when costs decline.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Competition intensity and inventory turnover become monitorable proxies for how quickly falling crude reaches consumers and headline inflation.
insights.quote: This could reflect lags in inventory replacement, uncertainty about the persistence of crude oil price changes or weaker competitive pressure when costs decline.
insights.locator: This could reflect lags in inventory replacement

insights.claim: Euro area HICP energy inflation swung from -3.1% in February 2026 to 10.8% in May before easing to 8.5% in June, with fuel prices the driver of the increase.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A near-14-point swing in the energy component in three months is the dominant source of euro area headline inflation surprise and a live input to ECB rate expectations.
insights.quote: the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) for fuel drove the increase in the HICP for energy from -3.1% to 10.8% between February and May 2026 before it declined to 8.5% in June
insights.locator: Conclusions

insights.claim: Several euro area countries temporarily cut fuel excise duties during the 2026 shock — as they did after Russia invaded Ukraine — reducing duties by around 8% versus end-February, but in most cases these measures expired in June 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Expiry of the offsets in June creates a mechanical upward base effect on fuel HICP in H2 2026 independent of any move in crude.
insights.quote: Several countries have temporarily cut excise duties to dampen the inflationary impact from the energy shock for consumers, as they did after Russia invaded Ukraine.
insights.locator: Excise duties are taxes levied at a fixed amount

insights.claim: The euro area average VAT rate on fuel was cut from 20.7% to 18.9% during the 2026 shock, so the VAT component rose only 24% versus a larger increase in the underlying retail price.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Governments used both excise and VAT levers, meaning measured fuel inflation understates the underlying market shock and will re-accelerate as rates normalise.
insights.quote: The VAT component increased by 24% compared with the end of February (hence less than the retail price percentage change due to a cut of around 8% to the average VAT rate across the euro area, from 20.7% to 18.9%).
insights.locator: Value added taxes (VAT) are levied as a fixed percentage

insights.claim: The ECB's overall verdict on the 2026 Middle East shock is that refining margins amplified an already large crude move into retail prices, while temporary tax reductions partially alleviated the consumer burden.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Frames the policy read: the inflation impulse was supply- and margin-driven and partly fiscally masked, arguing against treating it as evidence of durable demand-side inflation.
insights.quote: The Middle East oil price shock has been significant and had a marked impact on retail fuel prices, with refining margins amplifying the effect.
insights.locator: Conclusions
